body: Jackson City Council Public Safety & Parks Committee
title: Public Safety & Parks Committee Meeting

blocks.text: I would like to call to a public safety community meeting for September 10th, 2026 to order. Colleagues, are there any open introductions? Okay, next we will discuss agenda item number one, officer retention and recruitment. Chief Bratney, if you would approach the podium. You may want to sit down. Or sit down, whatever make you comfortable. Okay, Lynn, we'll start off. Whichever way you want to go, you all can answer your first question if you have any. You can. Thank you. How is retention and recruitment going? Thank you, ma'am.

I appreciate you. Rochelle Brackney, Chief of Police Jackson PD. So we are currently poisoning ourselves to have another October class that we have on. If you would like the statistics, I can help you out with that if you allow me the benefit of putting on my glasses to get us to where our current status is. I just actually inquired about where we were and how we were going to be moving forward, since we do recoup our costs from the state to a large degree, it's about $4,500 or so an officer that we put through regardless of what jurisdiction that they are coming to us from.

And so the latest numbers that I just got from our chief is that we have currently, one second I'll pull the numbers up. We currently have five that we know that are definitely coming that have already cleared all of the paperwork and they're now doing the psychological exam. We have another six that just went through the physical fitness assessment as well. And then there's another seven that are taking the test and so we're in various phases of it. With other departments that are sending them to us, we are looking to host between our departments and there's 33 individuals minimum at this academy class coming through in October. We had nine that just graduated from the Academy in which all nine entered into FTO training. We have had to discontinue the employment of one and then there we are also evaluating the possibility of having to discontinue the employment of others in that class.

In terms of our resignations and our retirements that are going on, they are at the normal levels in terms of retirement. Recruitment efforts, we have now, and then I just got an email from Director Toya Martin where Alcorn State does an annual fair here, but we have already been in conversations and talks to have a direct pipeline from them to JPD setting up a program with Alcorn to be able to come directly from a cadet style program into Jackson Police Department. We do not currently have an established cadet program that has been used as a pipeline into the organization.

Now the one thing you have to understand is that traditionally four year institutions and job fairs are not the places that will net you the recruitment opportunities that you would want because as we all know this is a very competitive field if a person comes out with a four year degree or with a master's degree, the thought about doing public service or civil service work has waned very differently and thus the original programs of Teach for America are that came into place so that you would have to do government service in order to get loan forgiveness and things of that nature.

There are things that we can do to recruit. Loan forgiveness is often one for public safety if you've done public service for 10 years and you've paid them that you can waive loans. But there's very stringent conditions often to that, which means 120 consecutive payments for your loans back. And so us being able to possibly offer partial loan forgiveness if a person applies for it is a great recruitment effort. You're also looking at, is there ways that we can recruit successfully if you speak a second language, if you have a degree, if you have an additional skill set that you already come with that we could offer one time sign on bonuses that allow you after you sign on the first six months you're successful, you get half of it and then the other six months you get the other half of that bonus.

And it then builds in recruitment and retention. For recruitment and retention efforts, I recently just put out notices for anyone who is interested in a specialty assignment or creating a pathway to additional duties and responsibilities beyond patrol, whether it was investigations, crime scene analysis, intelligence analysis, task force officers, so that we could see who was interested in staying in the organization but also wanted additional support that received an overwhelming response from within the organization as we did that. I also just put out recently for professional development for the first time if any of our lieutenants, captains or deputy chiefs were interested in attending the IACP, the International Association Chief of Police Conference, that we could support that kind of development.

And then we also are taking applications for the FBI National Academy that the FBI has offered and said that Jackson will have one slot. I'm hoping to get at least one a year. And so we are now in the process of allowing opportunities for people to be developed further. As part of this recruitment and retention efforts, we're also looking at if we send you to a specialized training that costs the city a certain amount of money, that we be able to sign a contract with you that you stay with us, and then if you do not stay, it's prorated in which you reimburse the city.

We've had a lot of individuals who we have trained and have had this high level of training only to complete the training and go to another agency and then take their training with us. So the ability to retain talent is one of the things that we are looking at. In addition, ability to retain talent, we have presented a proposal to HR about a complete health and wellness initiative within Jackson Police Department in which we would phase Jackson Police Department and then phase two would also be fire and public works.

Those jobs that need a lot of support around physical fitness, mental health, stress, etc. We've presented that for result proposal because not only is HR can be supportive but we also understand that our current insurance providers will give us support and dollars for that that would be cost neutral to the city there would be no cost to the city whatsoever but there is a benefit to our officers. That would include developing a particular app for this initiative that we could have for each of the different departments. It's wellness planning, it's assessments, physical assessments, accountability partners, meal prep, and discounted to the physical fitness facilities as well. So there are quite a few things that we are doing to continue to engage officers but also to offer individuals who want to come to our communities that we are doing some of the more innovative creative things here as well. Continuing another area that we're looking at providing opportunities, as you know the city has just been awarded a grant to purchase two unmanned aerial devices or drones and

And part of that would be the opportunity to become a pilot of those aerial devices and how they would get the additional training. Officers and our younger individuals love technology. So knowing that there's more pathways to engage beyond the basic 911 call services, although we understand that is absolutely important, we do need to show people the ability to expand and to grow and to stretch and be a much more productive part of the community. So that's currently where we are and where we stand on our recruitment and our retention efforts.

Thank you, Chief. And this is something that I'm not familiar with myself. What is sort of an entry-level position, if you wanted to just join the police force, what are the minimum qualifications or requirements to be, for example, patrol officer and 911 dispatcher, or what are the entry level minimum qualifications? So the majority of them are high school education is what they're requiring, a GED or equivalent of a high school education for all of the positions. And 21 is normally the age for policing, but you can also get waivers if a person is younger than that and wants to apply because, you know, 21 is the year of age in which you can purchase a weapon or legitimately legally have a weapon.

The other one is just good physical conditions. You must be able to pass the physical fitness test as well as a background psychological test to say that if you have the temperament is what we are now looking for versus necessarily the old psychological test that they would give. There are now temperament tests that you can give that can determine whether the person has the temperament to work within the agency. After their physical fitness and their background checks, you know, they're going to look for things like, yes, they're going to ask about your credit history, but we also understand that people have credit histories for a variety of reasons.

If you are in a low wage position or if you have a medical history where you have back medical bills, those all can impact your credit. It's a very different standard. We are looking for a person who has a valid driver's license, which is a mandatory valid driver's license that is active at the point of time in which they are to be employed with the agency. And then they will also do a competency test. Most of the barriers that we are finding for individuals who want to get into policing is that they believe that the only way they can have a pathway into supporting us is as a uniform.

You can come into support JPD, animal control, you can come in through as a criminalist and so we're looking to civilianize a lot of our positions where people have the expertise to do that work so that we can then have officers who are doing those positions respond to 911 calls and to investigations differently. We do currently have more staff in those kind of administrative positions that we would like to have based on someone being able to fulfill those requirements. You can also enter into a pathway as a park ranger.

There are lots of ways, animal control, you can be a PSA administrative assistant, criminologist, police tech, EOC, 911 operator, detention officer. There are so many pathways into working for JPD. It doesn't always translate to a uniform, but those are the support systems that we need in place in order for the officers who are in uniformed investigations to do their work. Thank you. So you mentioned that there was five that were cleared and ready to begin the program in October. Six additional on the physical fitness. and we're doing sort of other testing, and then sort of combined with other agencies, we'll have 33, but of course, all of those won't be coming to JPD.

But to hear that there's probably gonna be, say, five to 20 that will be coming through JPD, I think is a really good sign. What is our current number of sworn officers that we have? So that number is currently hovering around 208. So we have lost a four additional officers since our last reporting of 212, again, for a variety of reasons. And the one thing that I am doing so that we can reconcile our stats when people ask us how many retirements have we had, how many resignations have we had, or why they're leaving.

Although we're putting into a place for exit interviews and things of that nature, I am documenting on the notes the reasons that we were told they were leaving. And more recently the ration of resignations, I've had three. Beside each of those I put that that officer was under investigation when they resigned. And so that we're being able to track better that it doesn't just look like they resigned and left the agency that the reasons we understand that they are resigning. If they're going for other employment and we know they're going to another agency, that they're resigning and then went to another agency so that we can track as much as we can as we start to put in systems for doing that.

What are some of the reasons that they're putting in or the investigations? Can you mention, generally, without us having to go into an executive session or not? I can say that when a person is under investigation, and hopefully I can phrase it in a way that would be understanding, if a person is under investigation serious enough that they resign versus facing the internal affairs investigation, there's probably a connection to some criminality that they're worried about that this is going to either end in their termination or into a criminal charge.

Is that helpful? Yes, is there any patterns or anything like that you're seeing? Do we have a pattern of perhaps, you know, poor performance or something illegal going on? Do we see a pattern in a way that you can put your hands, put your finger on? I think two areas that, possibly three. And what do I mean by that? One of them would be say, neglect of duty. Their inability or have not done the work in which they have been, thank you, in which they have been paid to do.

Incomplete reports, incomplete investigations, no follow-ups on those investigations. Another area I would say is upon review of their behaviors, body-worn cameras and things of that nature, is there a possibility that when we are done with our investigations that we will be presenting that information, internal affairs information to the District Attorney's Office is how I will phrase that. The other way is that more recent, is there a possibility that resources were not appropriately used within the agency? So those are four different reasons, resource? Resources, I would put those all in kind of the same one.

with the DA? That would be correct, sir. When you say resources, are you saying the officers? I believe this would probably be better for an executive session. Chief, as he was speaking, it gave me reminders of my own work in the school system, and obviously there's many, many, many differences there. But I think one similarity that that struck me as is the need to train up the folks that you have. And it's almost sad to say that in some ways because like when Microsoft hires a computer coder, they don't then teach them how to code.

They assume that they have those skills and the education and the programs that they've done have equipped them with there. And so when Microsoft hires a coder, they just give them a project. They say, here, go code this and folks go do it. When I was in school, since my father, even when I hired a teacher who was a degree professional, who had gone through a program to teach them how to be a teacher, many educators struggled with basic lesson planning, basics of classroom management, basics of how to work with parents and families, and some of these basics.

And I found that I almost had to assume that, OK, I'm going to have to teach you what you need to know. Because I was in the position to say, if you don't meet these standards, then you can't work because I wouldn't have had any teachers. And so I'd imagine that you probably are finding yourself having to do a lot of upscaling and training as well. And I had, just for the record, I had amazing teachers who were not dumb, they weren't, I mean, they were good, hardworking, they cared, they weren't apathetic, they were very smart, they were trying their best, but the programs that trained them had failed them.

And so I found that we had to, now obviously you have some that aren't willing to do it and you've got to make adjustments, but I imagine you're in a situation where There's probably going to have to be a lot of upscaling and training that needs to occur. Yes, we are not only on the most basic, one of the questions I just recently asked about policies and procedures. What was our mechanism for making sure that our employees, one, received the policy, understood the policy, and have been trained on the policy?

And so the answer I got back was, well, we gave them the policy on this date. And so much like your Microsoft example, if I'm just given the policy, I'm not trained on the policy, and then asked if I understand the policy, and then how do you operationalize the policy that is in front of you, all we are guaranteeing is that we handed them the policy. And so that is where we are now having to change the way that we even go about the work. Another example is at the training academy.

I've asked specifically what are the lesson plans for each and every session and curriculum that we have on file. Do we have those lesson plans? Do we also have the CV, resume, bio, whatever it is of the person who's teaching it? And are we attaching that to the lesson plan so that when the first time anyone, and I'm not a lawyer here and I'll defer to the CAO, but the first time someone has an event with an officer, they're going to ask what was their training records, how were they trained, Who trained them?

Did they understand the training? Did they understand the policies? And what is the way in which we verify that they understood what was happening? And so there is a lot of disconnect in that way where we are having to train up. Again, not because that an individual may not have the capacity to understand, but have we set up systems to make sure they understand the information that is being given to them. Okay. My question is this, and I'll start off with the war story too. I taught leadership around the country for supervisors. One of the things I stressed is that anytime we go towards termination, we have to give that up at individual opportunity.

And that is a part of, I think, our EEOC regulations. That's a part of our, hopefully a part of our personnel regulations as well. And that is you bring the issue to the individual, you describe it, you tell them how they are falling short, you give them a period of time and check back with them and see if they're still out of compliance. and then you proceed on with that paperwork trail. And in this case, to make sure the city of Jackson is not held in a liable situation.

My question is this. Are you interacting with HR to make sure all of these individuals receive or we're following the book, we're following our procedures before we terminate someone so that we don't put the city in any type of jeopardy? Thank you. I spend a lot of time talking with Director Martin as well as Monica Clay who is assigned to us as well as Attorney Drew Martin about all of our policies and procedures. One to make sure that A, we have standardized policies and procedures is how we do our terminations.

The first ones, as we know, if you are a probationary employee, I do not need to give you a reason as to why we are terminating an individual. If a person has achieved civil service status and you are putting something like a performance plan into existence, do we have a standardized performance improvement plan model that we're not only using throughout the city but also within Jackson Police Department and does everybody understand what a performance improvement plan might be in terms of it's actually a lot more even in-depth president than even what you put down.

as a row of things. Any performance improvement plan should, one, yes, identify the problem. Two, you then talk to the employee and you have to get the employee to agree and understand that this is a problem. And then you have to come to up with a plan, again, that the employee understands and agrees to that this is the plan that will get you to your desired outcome. And you don't just check back with them individually as, hey, how's it going? You have to have regular meetings with them to see where they are on the plan and if there's been any barriers or obstacles to them being successful with the plan.

So it is really in depth in order to get a person to the final outcome of that. What I have found in the short period of time, the few people who have been on a PIP at JPD is there has not been a full understanding of how you pull out or how you create a performance improvement plan with them. So we are working with what do those steps look like, what does a plan look like, but more importantly, is there training that's coming from a centralized location like HR to create performance improvement plans and what are those individual steps that we do that.

So creating processes within JPD, but also creating processes across the city because they are civil service employees that meet the civil service standards. And I appreciate that. Just a quick question. I know when I was a supervisor, we had to do a evaluation a quarter on the officer on their performance. Do we still do that? So and I've not seen any come up yet through my time to see have they come up and where we are in evaluation quarter. So I'm not sure where we are in the evaluation process, right?

If it was January through April, are they now in a May through September? So, my arrival here would be where either they would have ended one or they would be now starting into a second quarter of that. But I can make sure that whatever that answer is, if they are stored doing formal evaluations in the manner in which there is a form that they're filling out that says we met with them and we checked with them, et cetera. What I have asked each of the supervisors to do is to create an electronic folder on each of their officers who are underneath them so that when you're having conversations with them, you can easily document that.

It's all part of a folder and then you can all get them to agree. They do put things on their daily activity reports when they interact with it, but you also need to make sure that you have that supporting documentation so that you can find it very quickly, very easily when it comes to evaluation time. Chief. And quick question. When you was talking about the policy book, now you know they have a handbook and they have the general orders and you were saying that you were trying to make sure all of them was educated on it.

Which one was you talking about? So ours are on the general orders. They do get the HR handbook in which they're giving them and I know we educate and should be educating on general orders that are changing. If there are any HR handbook policies, I would defer to the experts in HR that they should be the ones that are conducting the HR training if there's been a law change. I know we do get emails out that say there are law changes. Even more recently, Mississippi law has changed on whether you can terminate an officer for positive drug usage and how you have to terminate an officer.

So I just got that memo weld and we immediately had to put that to the test. And so immediately putting that to the test, it then gives the officer to say that you've been drug tested positively and you have an opportunity to now contest that and you have five days to decide whether you want to contest it or whether you want to go forward with a regular disciplinary action review. Literally that day we're testing it out, the policy. This officer decided not to contest the review.

He would then also then put himself back into the disciplinary action committee process that officer chose to resign. So instead, my resignation says, resigned under investigation. And so that's the kind of stringency in which I'm looking at coordinating with our legal department as well as our HR department. If we talk about retention, you know, I think broadly speaking across any industry, retention comes down to two things. It comes down to how much money they're making and then everything else. And in everything else, one of the big factors is their immediate supervisor.

And you hear this all the time that people don't leave jobs, they leave managers. And so some of that is just these soft skills of do you build relationships? Of course you have to challenge your direct reports. It's not all candy and rainbows and sunshine and kumbaya. But nonetheless, people should still feel like they're being supported. They should always feel like they're being respected. They should all never feel like they're being talked down to. They should, I mean, you should, there should be some sort of, again, you don't have to be best friends and, you know, do all that stuff, but there should be some sort of decorum and respect there.

Do you feel like you, from the whole, from yourself all the way down to all the managers and supervisors, is that something that you feel you're there, the department needs to grow a little bit there, because we're doing as much as we can on the money side and we're working there. But on the other side is, you know, sometimes people will even go to positions where they're making less money sometimes if they're feeling like they have conflict with their manager. So I think I would address that on two fronts, right? There are legitimate reasons for people to not feel respected in the workplace.

But there are also off-ramps that we are providing within the city that allows an individual who doesn't like a supervisor's tone or perceived tone, they get to file a grievance here in the city of Jackson for any complaint that they have. And we've not been able to bifurcate what does an actual grievance look like, and again I I will defer to the attorneys that would fall under an EEO complaint, right, discrimination, harassment and things of that nature. And we'll say, and I'll see, and I've seen these come up through this, I want to file a grievance because I don't like the tone that my sergeant gave me when they told me to go work in another precinct.

And so I'm refusing at, and next thing you know it comes in as a grievance out of HR, out of EEO. And so the response, there's that one. The second thing I would also suggest is, are we at any level? I don't think there's anybody, and I just think it's ironic we're having the discussion about decorum too soon sometimes, as we like to say. But I think there is also an opportunity for all of us to grow. As you know, we brought before this council the opportunity to have a formalized sergeants testing examination.

There had not been a testing examination in JPD since 2020, early 2021. We're almost seven years in so that the supervisors, the majority of them who are in the sergeants position, that frontline supervisor are in acting positions. They have not tested or assessed to the level of being a frontline supervisor. And I don't know what support they received prior to that position or those assignments. I don't know what the criterion was. I'm not suggesting that there was anything nefarious. I'm just suggesting that there was not a formal process that I understand or know to have identified them to be a frontline supervisor.

So this council approved us to be able to do an outside formal assessment, sergeant's examination through civil service. And I think that will help us in some ways because it will then be able to assess the the ability to do the work and not feel as though they've just been given the work and no support, no assessment of their ability to do the work. And if I can clarify just for the record, the company that was selected is not the company that was hired to do my chief search.

The company that was hired to do my chief search was the police executive research I know that was entered into council as saying that that was that is not correct that is different than the company that is doing The sergeants examination and won the request for proposal. Okay chief Right now is very competitive out there Getting recruits in a lot of times and I'm not advising folks to do this but if they're not fully committed to the city then they can go other places, make more money, and have less work. So it's very competitive and and this young man right here has been, he has been not making friends trying to get your numbers up, okay, but it's incumbent that we stop going towards the negative and start getting folks positively in place and keeping them in place because right now 208 is just not where anywhere close to where we want to be. This guy, he would take my lunch money to give you a couple million dollars.

And we don't want that because then that would spike my crime. But can I just say this, I am committed to the most professional police force, but I have said this over and over, although we may be desperate to hire, we will not hire desperately. That has gotten us into the problems that we are in today where we are having to terminate officers for ethical violations, for background histories we should have excluded from the beginning. I will take 200 quality officers who this community can trust. Then 275 officers, where 75 of them could be on the other side of that arrest. So I can appreciate that we may be going to the negative, but if it means getting us to the quality officers, officers who are not out there violating their civil rights, officers who are not out there committing acts of crimes and violence themselves. I can appreciate we're going to go down, but I can imagine that we're going to go down a little further before we get to the ability to do this. And 200

dedicated officers over 275 just to meet a number will never be something that is support, ever. Okay, and look, I'm not trying to insinuate that we're out there. That's not where I'm going with this. has to be a balance between this council trying pull out all stops to give you money to help and and and so if if you don't need a certain number then just make it clear that you don't need those that number and so we can stop we can stop that's not what I said I said I gave numbers that we need I gave very specific numbers said 275, this is what it will cost, 265, this is what it will cost, 255, this is what it will cost. I know what we need to do this work. Give me one second, sir. We're doing 1.4 million in overtime. So we know what we need to do this work. There are officers out here doing the work, but I will never sacrifice the integrity to have a number. It just can't happen and to have to decide, and I don't want it to feel this

way, but to decide what level of corruption that I can tolerate within the agency to get me a number, that number will go down every single time before I compromise the integrity, the ethics of the Jackson Police Department. The City of Jackson deserves better than that. And I agree. Thank you. 100% thank you if an officer is out there they found two officers in another Municipality close by new municipality using drugs and they busted them there in the park If we have officers on the take they gotta go if we got officers violating the law they need to go And so I agree wholeheartedly all I'm saying is We need to get good quality officers in the seat to help out those ones that are already there.

We agree. Can I phrase it this way? Because I love, I agree with what you're saying. And so I think the real question is, how fast can we get good officers? And so you've talked about a class in October, which believe it or not, it's like blink your eyes, it's practically October. So I think we're there, how long does it take to get one up and running? Can we get another one by Christmas? Can we get another one by Valentine's Day? Before you answer, I want to ask you.

I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Go ahead. And before you answer, let me ask you. Yes, ma'am. It's a lot of good officers have left the department. What are we doing to try to reach – which I know you probably don't know who they are, but what are we doing to try to recruit them back? So the one thing that I would say is I have said over and over and over that we're hiring. I've said over and over again that if somebody is interested in returning back to Jackson Police Department to please put in their applications to do that work again.

They should be evaluated fairly and competently as well. I also understand that previously what has caused a lot of angst and morale issues within in JPD is that we were bringing back anybody, hiring anybody, putting them in any position and that cannot occur if we want to build morale and a quality and competent agency. Now what are we thinking about doing differently? As I've been talking to our academy staff, is this? Is there, and I'm going to, I please don't want to hear my staff behind me clapping, But we keep offering the traditional way of going through a police academy.

You have to stay at the academy, live at the academy for a certain period of time of 12 weeks. That is not always the model that works in 2027 when people might be able to go to night school. What might we do to hold academies at night where you don't stay overnight, where you come two or three days a week differently than staying there. That gets a very different population than the group that can afford to stay there who are interested in becoming police officers but can't afford to quit their day jobs to get the certification to do that work.

That is a model that could work for us to bring people in into and recruit very differently than before. How can we also think about, much like we do, we've had to transition to online classes, virtual classes. Not everyone can get into the same space, but we also know that you can learn. So is it possible that we do some of the stuff virtually and some of the things in person hybrid so that we can create the best environment? Is it also that we may even need to change the way we do it now, two weeks on where you You come for the first couple of weeks to stay at the academy and then you return unless you're one of those persons who's coming to our academy from another jurisdiction where that three hour drive just isn't feasible.

We could provide you with accommodations. There are so many things that we can do to bring people into it faster, stronger, and more prepared to join Jackson Police Department as long as we're flexible and can accommodate the needs of 2027 and not the model from 1980. What I will say is they did try that once, having a class that went home every day. And I'm gonna say this, but being a trained officer, they didn't have any type of discipline, none whatsoever. And I'm not knocking your ideas, I promise I'm not, but they didn't have any kind of discipline.

And so that's my point. If we have to babysit our officers for 12 weeks in order that they have disappeared to be a police officer, again, is that the temperament we want? Because the moment they're not being babysat on day 1201 of week 1201, what is the behavior that we're experiencing? And so I'm going to suggest that maybe we're enabling them. Not everybody who applies to be a police officer should be one or should be accepted. But we should be doing the things that we can do to make sure they're prepared to do the work out there on the streets that everybody called to do.

So I heard that before and they said, oh, the reason we do it, we have officers stay overnight with our recruits to babysit recruits overnight. And so I'm starting to say to myself, is this the model that works best for Jackson or is it creating behaviors that may be difficult for us to correct in the end? Because we just had a class and now I may have three of them that will not make it out of probation. And we babysat them the whole time. And I will say this, I'm willing to try.

And it may was at the time they were hiring anything. They were. I agree with you. And it's a new day. No, I'm saying you're right. It's a new day that we are being very selective about who we invite into our Jackson Police Department and who we invite into this city to protect them. Okay. Thank you. Thank you chief for being here today. Thank you sir for inviting us here. A couple of questions on sworn officers. You said we have 208 sworn officers. Right about two-eight.

How many of them are patrol officers? I would have to do the quick math for you if you don't mind. Sure. Okay. Of those we're looking at about 130 of them are in patrol. So the majority of them are in patrol. Okay, so those are the ones that would be working out in the precincts, correct? That's correct, sir. index.summary: The Jackson City Council Public Safety and Parks Committee discussed police officer retention and recruitment with Chief Rochelle Brackney, who reported the department has about 208 sworn officers, with roughly 130 in patrol. She said an October academy class could bring in at least 33 recruits across agencies, with five already cleared and six more in testing. Brackney outlined recruitment and retention efforts including loan forgiveness, sign-on bonuses, specialty assignments, a health and wellness initiative, and a possible sergeant examination. The committee also discussed the Real-Time Command Center and camera system, with Brackney reporting many cameras are inoperable and that the center is understaffed. The committee agreed to pursue AI software and further review camera contracts, possibly in executive session.

topics.title: Officer retention and recruitment
topics.note: Chief Brackney reported about 208 sworn officers, with an October academy class expecting at least 33 recruits across agencies.

topics.title: Academy class and recruitment pipeline
topics.note: Five recruits cleared paperwork, six passed physical fitness, and seven are testing; Alcorn State pipeline discussed.

topics.title: Recruitment incentives
topics.note: Brackney proposed loan forgiveness, sign-on bonuses, and specialty assignments to attract and retain officers.

topics.title: Health and wellness initiative
topics.note: Proposal to HR for a phased wellness program for police, fire, and public works, intended to be cost-neutral.

topics.title: Drone program
topics.note: City awarded a grant to purchase two unmanned aerial devices; officers could train as pilots.

topics.title: Entry-level qualifications
topics.note: Minimum requirements include high school education or GED, age 21 with waivers possible, physical fitness, background and psychological tests.

topics.title: Civilian pathways in JPD
topics.note: Brackney listed non-uniform roles such as animal control, criminalist, 911 operator, and detention officer.

topics.title: Sworn officer count and resignations
topics.note: Sworn officers down to about 208 from 212; recent resignations included officers under investigation.

topics.title: Reasons for resignations
topics.note: Brackney cited neglect of duty, incomplete reports, body camera issues, and possible criminal referrals to the DA.

topics.title: Training and policy compliance
topics.note: Discussion on need for upscaling, lesson plans, and verifying officers understand policies.

topics.title: Termination procedures and HR coordination
topics.note: Brackney said she works with HR and legal on standardized termination and performance improvement plans.

topics.title: Performance evaluations
topics.note: Uncertainty about quarterly evaluations; Brackney asked supervisors to keep electronic folders on officers.

topics.title: Sergeant examination
topics.note: Council approved an outside formal sergeant examination through civil service; no testing since 2020-2021.

topics.title: Quality vs. quantity in hiring
topics.note: Brackney said she will not hire desperately and prefers 200 quality officers over 275 with integrity issues.

topics.title: Patrol staffing levels
topics.note: About 130 patrol officers across four precincts and three shifts, averaging roughly 11 per precinct per shift.

topics.title: Take-home vehicle policy
topics.note: Brackney clarified no new policy; city policy requires 24-hour employees and Hinds County residency unless approved.

topics.title: Real-Time Command Center staffing
topics.note: Center should be staffed by civilians; currently down to two positions, with four allocated and interviews underway.

topics.title: Camera system status
topics.note: Reported 88 operable and 84 inoperable city asset cameras; 58 operable and 20 inoperable LPR cameras; many donor cameras inoperable.

topics.title: AI software for cameras
topics.note: Demonstration of AI integration to pull data from multiple systems and send alerts; council supportive of moving forward.

topics.title: Camera costs and contracts
topics.note: JPD pays about $88 monthly for energy and $43 for AT&T per camera; CAO and chief reviewing contracts and grant funding.

topics.title: Drones for streetlight mapping
topics.note: Brackney suggested using new drones to identify streetlights that are out and report to public works.

topics.title: Future metrics and KPIs
topics.note: Committee will ask departments for metrics and key performance indicators after budget hearings.
